newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania president says cabinet reshuffle possible.
newsitem.headline: Romania president says cabinet reshuffle possible.

text.p: President Emil Constantinescu has suggested a cabinet reshuffle might be necessary to resolve disputes within Romania's coalition government over revising the 1997 budget to meet IMF demands.

In a television interview late on Thursday, Constantinescu said government reforms introduced since ex-communists were voted out of office last year were being held up by delays in closing down inefficient industry. But he expressed full confidence in Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea.
"Reform at the level of enterprises has not yet started and that is the hard core of reform, where people are affected by layoffs," he said.

"If this does not proceed as it should, I am prepared to preside over a cabinet meeting...as is my constitutional right. There will be reshuffles if they are necessary, if we see that one minister or another does not pass the test or a ministry is badly run. I have full confidence in the prime minister..."
Ministers have been bickering openly over revisions to the budget as required by the International Monetary Fund for new disbursements of credits to underpin reforms.

An IMF team has been in Bucharest since mid-July to determine whether the government has met reform targets to release the second of five $86 million credits under a 13-month standby arrangement approved in April.
The mission has made no public comment on progress in curbing inflation, proceeding with privatisation and closing down inefficient farms and industries.

Ciorbea's cabinet was due on Friday to hold a meeting, already postponed twice, to discuss budget revisions. No details on amendments have been announced but ministers have been publicly defending their allocations.
The prime minister has also been meeting trade unionists to allay their fears of mass job cuts, but top union leaders stormed out of a meeting on Thursday, saying the government was botching reforms.
They demanded the resignation of ministers linked to reform and asked Constantinescu to take part in further negotiations.
Despite some protests, including noisy rallies by restive coal miners, most unionists have backed the government's reform programme and refrained from work stoppages.
In his remarks on television, Constantinescu praised labour leaders "who have said they are ready to accept the sacrifice, the cost involved in reform."

The president, who defeated ex-communist Ion Iliescu in last year's election, appointed Ciorbea to head a government of Christian Democrats, Liberals, Social Democrats and members of the 1.6 million-strong ethnic Hungarian community.
It has freed prices, revamped foreign exchange markets and introduced laws to attract foreign investors. But ministers admit privatisation and restructuring are moving too slowly.

Monthly inflation, which peaked at more than 30 percent in March, is expected to slide below two percent in July. Ministers have pledged to keep the budget deficit within a target of 4.5 percent of gross domestic product.
